extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy (learners of classification, definitions, and semantics)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for classifying terms and forming definitions: logical meanings of genus/species, the roles of differentia/proprium/accidens, and how to construct complete vs. imperfect definitions. Aimed at guiding conceptual analysis and technical definition in philosophical logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus and Species (logical meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every class which is a real Kind is either a genus or a species: a Kind not divisible into other Kinds is a species; a Kind admitting division into real Kinds is a genus to those below and a species to those above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains predicability relations: the proximate Kind's properties comprehend those of all other Kinds predicable of the individual. A species which is not further divisible cannot be a genus. Examples: animal (genus) and man (species); genus includes species and denotes more individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia — standard account and problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentia is the attribute that distinguishes a given species from every other species of the same genus; but because a Kind is distinguished by an indefinite number of properties, there is a question which distinguishing attribute 'differentia' refers to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the Aristotelian requirement that the differentia be part of the essence. Raises the issue that many distinguishing attributes exist (e.g., rationality vs. cooking) and that selection of a differentia depends on which connoted attributes are taken as essential by language or usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia grounded in connotation, not metaphysical essence
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between Differentia, Proprium, and Accidens is founded in the connotation of names rather than in the intrinsic nature of things; the differentia is the surplus of connotation which the species has over the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational rule: Differentia = that which must be added to the connotation of the genus to complete the connotation of the species. Example: 'man' connotes all that 'animal' does plus rationality and some outward form; those surplus connotations are the differentia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia may vary by classificatory purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A species referred to the same genus will not always have the same differentia; the differentia depends on the principle and purpose governing the particular classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical taxonomy may choose different bases (warm-blooded vs. cold-blooded; lungs vs. gills; dentition and posture) depending on the naturalist's purposes. Names can acquire a special technical connotation in a scientific context distinct from ordinary use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprium (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proprium is an attribute which belongs to all individuals of the species and, though not connoted by the specific name, follows necessarily from some attribute that the name does connote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proprium differs from essence (not part of the connotation) but is necessarily consequent on the connoted attributes. Example by demonstration: in a parallelogram, opposite sides equal. Example by causation: understanding language follows from rationality in man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of Proprium (demonstrative and causal)
rubrics_metrics.description: One Proprium may follow from connoted attributes as a demonstrative inference (conclusion from premises) or as an effect following a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrative example: properties of a parallelogram that can be proved from its defining attributes. Causal example: capacity for language follows causally from rationality. Both are necessary consequences under accepted laws of inference or nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidens (definition; separable vs. inseparable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidens includes attributes neither involved in the signification of the name nor known to have any necessary connection with the connoted attributes; they are commonly divided into separable and inseparable accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accidents have no necessary bearing on the essence. Inseparable accidents are universal in known instances but not logically necessary; separable accidents are sometimes absent (or vary over time or individuals). Examples discussed below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inseparable accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Inseparable accidents are properties universal to the known instances of a species but not connoted by the name and not known to be logically necessary; they could conceivably be absent without altering the species' definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: blackness in crows — universal in known crows but not part of the connotation 'crow'; if white crows were discovered they would be 'white crows' rather than non-crows. Thus inseparable accidents are empirically universal but not definitional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separable accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Separable accidents are attributes that are sometimes absent from individuals of the species, or not constant in the same individual; they are neither necessary nor universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: colour of an European (varies among humans), being born (an attribute only at one time), or transient states like being hot/cold, sitting/walking. These are clearly accidental and do not enter into definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as a proposition declaratory of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A Definition is a proposition which declares the meaning of a word — either the common acceptation or the special meaning the speaker/writer intends to annex for the purpose of discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that definitions are verbal and serve to specify the connotation (what the name involves). A correct definition should make known what the term signifies in the intended context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names are undefinable
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names, being mere marks put upon individuals and lacking connotation, cannot be defined; propositions that merely identify the individual are not definitions of the name's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: 'John Thomson is the son of General Thomson' or 'the man now crossing the street' indicate who is referred to but do not define the proper name. Identification differs from definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining connotative names: direct and indirect modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Connotative names are defined by declaring their connotation either directly (by enumerating the attributes) or indirectly (by predicating synonymous names or by per genus et differentiam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct form: 'Man is everything which possesses corporeity, organization, life, rationality, and a form…' Indirect: using synonyms ('Man is a human being') or composing genus + differentiae. The direct form is most precise but often too technical/verbose for ordinary use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as analysis (complete definition requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete definition is the sum total of all essential propositions which can be framed with that name as subject; it should enable deriving all propositions implied by the name without other premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition = analysis: resolving a complex signification into constituent attributes. A truly adequate definition declares all facts connoted by the name. Exceptions: names of simple feelings (elementary sensations) cannot be analysed and so resist full verbal definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect/unscientific definitions: essential-incomplete vs accidental (descriptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ordinary definitions aim only to guide correct use and therefore may be imperfect: (a) Essential but incomplete definitions (state part of connotation), or (b) Accidental/descriptive definitions (state something not part of the connotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of essential-incomplete: 'Man is a rational animal' — adequate for present-known objects but incomplete because it omits other connoted attributes and may be overturned by new discoveries. Logician's rule 'per genus et differentiam' often results in incomplete definitions when differentia is taken narrowly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining abstract names and single attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract name expresses a single attribute, its definition must appeal to the underlying phenomenon (the 'foundation' of the attribute) and analyse that phenomenon into parts if complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the attribute is grounded in a complex phenomenon (e.g., eloquence), definition should dissect cause and effect (eloquence = power of influencing affections by speech or writing). If the attribute is a simple feeling (e.g., sensation of white), verbal definition ultimately appeals to shared experience rather than further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of per genus et differentiam and summum genus
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that a definition must be per genus et differentiam is not always tenable (e.g., for the highest genus with no superior genus); nevertheless, most names (except names of simple feelings) admit of definition by analysing constituent facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges historical logician rules but insists on the broader analytic account: define by setting forth constituent attributes or the facts underlying an attribute; where analysis cannot proceed (simple sensations), direct appeal to experience is required.
